tagline.text: A city of love flowing between batchoy and old mansions

children.text: The central city of Panay Island, which flourished on the Spanish-era sugar trade. It's a great food-and-walking city in the Visayas, where you can stroll and eat your way through the old shopping street Calle Real, the riverside Esplanade, historic churches, and La Paz batchoy.

Iloilo City is the central city of the Western Visayas region, in the southeast of Panay Island facing the Guimaras Strait. It flourished as a sugar and textile trading port during the Spanish colonial era in the 19th century, ranking as the richest city after Manila, and in

it received the title "La Muy Leal y Noble Ciudad" (the Most Loyal and Noble City) from the Spanish crown. Stone mansions and shop buildings built by sugar barons of that era, along with beautiful churches, still stand throughout the city today.

The city is divided into districts based on its old town units — City Proper, Molo, Jaro, La Paz, Mandurriao, Arevalo, Lapuz, and others. Each district has its own plaza, church, and signature dish, making it fun to explore the city district by district. More recently, a large mixed-use development has risen on the site of the old airport in Mandurriao district, giving the city a modern skyline.

The people of Iloilo, known as Ilonggos, are famous for their soft, gentle way of speaking, which has earned the city the nickname "City of Love." It's often cited as one of the most livable cities in the Philippines thanks to its cleanliness and well-developed bike lanes and riverside paths, and it gets high marks among Korean expats and long-term residents too.

It suits travelers who enjoy walking, eating, and sightseeing over flashy tourist attractions, and those interested in historic architecture and churches. It's also a good starting point for a West Visayas trip that continues on to Guimaras, Miagao, Islas de Gigantes, and Bacolod.
In
, Iloilo became the first city in the Philippines to join the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in the field of gastronomy. With a population of about 470,000 in the
census, it is the largest city on Panay Island, and along the Iloilo River that runs through the city center stretches the Esplanade, whose first section opened in

and which is considered the longest linear park in the Philippines. The old commercial street Calle Real is a component of the "Negros–Panay Sugar Cultural Landscape," which was placed on the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in
La Paz batchoy, a rich noodle soup topped with pork offal, liver, and crispy fried pork skin, is Iloilo's signature dish. You can try a bowl for about
at the old batchoy shops inside La Paz Market.

An old commercial district centered on J.M. Basa Street, lined with restored early-20th-century neoclassical and art deco shophouses. It's especially nice to walk here at dusk when the lights come on.

A Gothic Revival church built of coral stone, nicknamed the "feminist church" because the statues lining its interior columns depict only female saints. Try pancit Molo, a clear dumpling soup, nearby.
A cathedral dedicated to Our Lady of Candelaria, notable for its bell tower standing separately in the plaza across the street. A major celebration is held here every
February 2
for the Feast of Candelaria.
A riverside promenade stretching for several kilometers, where mangroves meet city views. It's a favorite spot for an early morning jog or an evening stroll.

blocks.title: See the old mansions of Jaro

children.text: Mansions built by sugar barons, such as Nelly's Garden, are clustered in Jaro district. Most are private property, so it's best to admire them from the outside, but check whether there are open events or pre-booked tours.
A 19th-century stone mansion in Arevalo district, now a living museum where you can experience the daily life and traditional food of an old Ilonggo household. Booking ahead may be required.
A Santo Niño festival held around the fourth weekend of
January
each year, when dance troupes in tribal costume fill the whole city with a dynamic parade.
Batchoy for breakfast at La Paz Market, followed by local coffee at a nearby old café
Jaro Cathedral and its belfry, admire the old mansion exteriors around Jaro Plaza
Buy snacks like biscocho at an old bakery in Jaro
Molo Church and Molo Plaza, a late lunch of pancit Molo
Stroll Calle Real heritage street, visit a museum
Sunset walk along the Iloilo River Esplanade
Seafood or chicken inasal in the Mandurriao restaurant district
Take a bangka day trip to Guimaras from Parola wharf, or visit Miagao Church to the south

children.text: The National Museum Western Visayas Regional Museum occupies the old provincial jail building built in
, where you can see elephant and Stegodon fossils found on Panay Island and an exhibit on Iloilo's textile industry. Admission is free, and it is closed on Mondays.
At the Museum of Philippine Economic History (free), housed in the old Elizalde building on Calle Real, you can learn about the era of the sugar trade.
Have lunch of batchoy at La Paz Market, then drink cloth-filtered coffee at Madge Café. A cup costs about
Visit the Iloilo Museum of Contemporary Art (ILOMOCA) at Festive Walk. It is open Tuesday–Sunday,
, and closed on Mondays.
Visit Camiña Balay nga Bato in Arevalo. The house was built in
and was designated an Important Cultural Property by the National Museum in
. Call ahead to check the visiting hours.
At La Paz Market, pick one or two of Netong's, Ted's, and Deco's and try the batchoy.
Buy biscocho at a bakery in Jaro, then walk around Jaro Plaza to see the cathedral and belfry.
Have a light lunch in City Proper with Roberto's jumbo siopao.
Enjoy a bowl of pancit Molo around Molo Plaza and see Molo Church.
Have dinner of grilled seafood and KBL at Breakthrough or Tatoy's on the Arevalo waterfront. Many reviews say Tatoy's requires reservations on weekends.
Stroll along the Festive Walk Parade in Mandurriao and enjoy the nightlife atmosphere. Smallville Complex is home to a cluster of bars and clubs.
It's about
1 hour 10 minutes

from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO), with several daily flights on Philippine Airlines, Cebu Pacific, and AirAsia. There are also direct flights from Cebu, Davao, Cagayan de Oro, and elsewhere.
The airport is in Cabatuan, about
from the city center. Airport shuttle vans have no timetable and leave when full, costing about
per person; Grab (4-seater) costs about

From Cebu there is a direct flight of about
40–50 minutes
, and for international routes, direct flights to Singapore (Scoot) and Hong Kong are either operating or about to resume. Schedules change often, so check the airline's latest announcements.
A fast craft from Bacolod takes about

and costs about

Large passenger ferries also sail from Manila, but the trip takes over
20 hours

The dry season, from
December
to
May
, is best for exploring the city on foot.
December–February
is relatively cool, while
March–May
is hot, so it's better to plan activities for the morning and evening rather than midday. From
June
to
November
is the rainy season with frequent showers, but few days see rain all day long, so city sightseeing is still quite feasible. Typhoons mainly affect the area during
August–November
During the Dinagyang Festival, around the fourth weekend of
January
, accommodation books up months in advance and roads are closed, so book early if you want to see the festival, or avoid this period otherwise. The Jaro Candelaria Festival on
February 2
and Holy Week events in
April
are also worth seeing.
Daytime highs start around
in
January
and climb steadily, peaking around
in
April
, the hottest month. Annual rainfall is about 2,150 mm, with
July
the wettest and
March–April

almost rain-free. In the rainy season, low-lying areas such as Jaro, Arevalo, and La Paz often flood when heavy rain coincides with high tide. Dozens of villages (barangays) were flooded during Typhoon Uwan and Tropical Depression Verbena in
November 2025
, and again during heavy rains in the
rainy season.

Accommodation splits broadly into two areas. The City Proper area near Calle Real and the river is great for walking and soaking up the old-town atmosphere, while the new downtown in Mandurriao district is convenient, with large malls, chain hotels, and a restaurant strip. Mid-range hotels run about
a night, business hotels
and up, and there are also many Airbnb-style condos.

Iloilo is one of the top food cities in the Philippines. Beyond La Paz batchoy, signature dishes include pancit Molo, a clear dumpling soup with shrimp and pork meatballs, crisp-baked treats like biscocho and butter cookies, and old-bakery snacks from Jaro district. Madge Café, which has operated inside La Paz Market since the
, is a traditional coffee shop beloved by locals, and the coastal Arevalo district is home to a cluster of seafood restaurants. Chicken inasal here is every bit as good as in Bacolod.
On the Arevalo waterfront, Breakthrough Restaurant (Molo–Arevalo Boulevard), which opened in

, is known for grilled fish and KBL (a soup of kadyos beans, pork, and jackfruit), and Tatoy's for native chicken and seafood. Roberto's in City Proper is famous for its Queen Siopao, and at Camiña Balay nga Bato in Arevalo you can reserve a meal of traditional cocoa and pancit Molo. At night, Mandurriao's Smallville Complex (bars, clubs, and restaurants) and the restaurant strip along the Festive Walk Parade, which stretches about
1.1 km
, get busy. For souvenir biscocho, a biscocho specialty shop in Jaro is a safe choice.
Churches and old mansions photograph best, and are less hot to visit, early in the morning or after
When visiting church interiors, wear clothing that covers your shoulders and knees, and avoid taking photos during Mass.
Many batchoy stalls open early in the morning and stay open late, making it a good breakfast option.
It's also nice to rent a bike and ride the length of the Esplanade. The city government has steadily expanded its bike lanes.
Grab is easy to find, but waiting times get longer during the rainy evening rush hour (
5–7 PM
), so allow extra time.
For souvenirs, a regional specialty shop inside a mall or a bakery in Jaro is a safe bet for biscocho, dried mango, and piaya pastries.
If you plan a day trip to Guimaras, leave from Parola wharf early in the morning to have enough time to look around properly.
The National Museum Western Visayas Regional Museum, housed in the former provincial jail building, and the Museum of Philippine Economic History are free, Museo Iloilo costs about
, and the Iloilo Museum of Contemporary Art (ILOMOCA) costs about
. Check in advance the days the National Museum is closed and how entry reservations work.
The main Dinagyang event (the Ati tribe competition) is held on the fourth Sunday of January every year. It fell on
January 25
in 2026 and falls on
January 24
in 2027. In 2026, about 550,000 people came over the three days. Reserved grandstand seats cost
in 2025 and sold out early, and in 2026 general seating at the Iloilo Sports Complex was sold from
. Check the official booking information early.
The National Museum Western Visayas Regional Museum is open Tuesday–Sunday,
(free admission), and ILOMOCA is open Tuesday–Sunday,
(adults
); both are closed on Mondays. Check the closing days of other museums in advance as well.
During the
June–November

rainy season, heavy rain coinciding with high tide can flood low-lying areas, and fast crafts and the Guimaras boat may be canceled. Check the weather and whether boats are running before you leave, and book flights and ferries on changeable terms.
The city is relatively safe, but watch out for pickpockets in crowded places like markets and terminals, and don't keep your phone in your back pocket.

Crowds during the Dinagyang Festival are enormous, so carry only minimal valuables and agree on a meeting point with your group in advance. Parade viewing areas are often run as paid seating, so check ahead.
Some roads can flood during the rainy season, so check the weather before heading into low-lying areas.
Many of the old mansions are private property. Don't climb over fences or enter without permission.
Some taxis do not use the meter and quote a flat fare, so confirm the fare before getting in or use Grab. During rush hour, Grab fares rise to 1.5–2 times the usual.
The risk of dengue rises in the rainy season, so avoid standing water and bring mosquito repellent.
